body.objective: Students will be able to name family members.
successCriteria: I can name family members in Spanish
I can use masculine and feminine family words
I can talk about who is in a family tree
body.hook: In many Spanish-speaking families, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins gather every Sunday for a big meal. Family is central, so family words are among the first you'll need.

study.title: Mi familia
study.question: Who is in a family?
study.passage:
Text (read aloud, written for this lesson):
¡Hola! Me llamo Diego. Esta es mi familia. Mi padre se llama Carlos y mi madre se llama Ana. Tengo una hermana, Sofía, y un hermano, Mateo. Mis abuelos se llaman José y Rosa. Mi tío Luis es el hermano de mi madre. Tengo dos primos, Pablo y Elena. ¡Mi familia es grande!
Grammar: masculine -o, feminine -a: hermano/hermana, tío/tía, primo/prima.
Plurals: the masculine plural can include both genders: los hermanos = brothers or brothers and sisters; los padres = parents; los abuelos = grandparents.
Possession with de: el hermano de mi madre (my mother's brother).
Activity: draw a family tree (real or of a famous/fictional family) and label it; then partners ask ¿Quién es…? and answer Es mi…
study.source: Original text written for this lesson.
steps: Draw and label a family tree
discussion: How many siblings does Diego have?
Why can "los hermanos" mean brothers and sisters?
How do you show possession with de?
study.product: Draw and label a family tree with at least eight family members in Spanish, and write four sentences about it.

practice.q: Why can los hermanos include sisters?
practice.a: A masculine plural can include both genders.

practice.q: Translate: My aunt is my mother's sister.
practice.a: Mi tía es la hermana de mi madre.

misconceptions: Thinking los padres means fathers only
exitTicket: Nombra cinco miembros de la familia.

options: A) la hermana de mi padre
C) la padre de mi hermana
items.answer: A) la hermana de mi padre

items.q: Name eight family members in Spanish.
items.answer: Padre, madre, hermano, hermana, abuelo, abuela, tío, tía.

items.q: Give feminine forms of hermano, tío and primo.
Who is Luis in the text?
Describe two people in your tree.

items.answer: The masculine plural can include both genders.

body.objective: Students will be able to use tener and possessive adjectives.
body.iCan: I can use tener and possessive adjectives.
successCriteria: I can conjugate tener in the present
I can use possessive adjectives mi, tu, su, nuestro
I can describe what family members have
body.hook: "Tengo dos hermanos. Mi hermano tiene un perro. Su perro es enorme." Tener (to have) and the words my, your and his/her let you talk about everyone in your life and what they have.

vocabulary.definition: I have / you have / he, she has

study.title: Tengo…
study.question: How do I say what people have and whose things are whose?
study.passage:
Grammar (written for this lesson):
tener (irregular): yo tengo, tú tienes, él/ella/usted tiene, nosotros tenemos, vosotros tenéis (Spain), ellos/ellas/ustedes tienen.
Possessive adjectives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: mi hermano, mis hermanos; tu gato, tus gatos; su perro (his/her/their dog), sus perros; nuestro abuelo, nuestra abuela, nuestros primos.
Text: Tengo una familia pequeña. Tengo un hermano. Mi hermano tiene quince años y tiene un perro. Su perro se llama Toby. Nosotros tenemos dos gatos también. Mis abuelos tienen una casa en Chile. ¿Y tú? ¿Tienes mascotas?
Negative: no + verb: No tengo hermanas.
Activity: "¿Tienes…?" survey: ask classmates about siblings and pets; report with tiene/tienen and su/sus.
study.source: Original text written for this lesson.
steps: Survey classmates about siblings and pets
discussion: How many pets does the family have?
Why is it "mis abuelos" with an s?
What does su mean in "su perro"?
study.product: Write six sentences about your family and pets using four forms of tener and four possessive adjectives.

practice.q: How old is the brother in the text?

practice.a: Possessives agree with the thing owned (abuela is feminine).
It can mean his, her, their or your (formal).

practice.q: Translate: My grandparents have a house in Chile.
practice.a: Mis abuelos tienen una casa en Chile.

practice.q: Write about your family and pets.

misconceptions: Making possessives agree with the owner

test.title: Practice test: Use tener and possessive adjectives

options: D) his, her, their or your
items.answer: D) his, her, their or your

items.q: Conjugate tener for yo, tú and él.
Conjugate tener for nosotros and ellos.
Report a survey answer with su.

items.answer: They agree with the thing owned.

body.objective: Students will be able to describe my family.
successCriteria: I can describe family members' appearance and personality
I can combine ser, tener and possessives in a description
I can present a family in Spanish
body.hook: Now you can put it all together: who's in your family, what they're like and what they have. Today you'll present your family (real, imagined or famous) in Spanish.

study.title: Te presento a mi familia
study.question: How do I describe my family in Spanish?
study.passage:
Model (written for this lesson):
Te presento a mi familia. Mi madre se llama Laura. Es alta y tiene el pelo castaño y los ojos verdes. Es muy trabajadora. Mi padre se llama Omar. Es bajo y tiene el pelo negro. Es divertido. Tengo una hermana menor. Se llama Mia, tiene ocho años y es cariñosa. Mi abuela vive con nosotros. Tiene el pelo gris y es muy simpática. ¡Me encanta mi familia!
Structures: ser + personality and height (Es alta, es divertido). tener + hair and eyes (Tiene el pelo rubio, tiene los ojos azules).
Order: in Spanish most adjectives come after the noun: el pelo negro, los ojos verdes.
Plural adjectives add -s: ojos azules.
Activity: create a poster or slide of a family (real, invented or a famous TV family) and present it in 1 minute. Classmates ask one question: ¿Cómo es tu…? ¿Cuántos años tiene…?
study.source: Original model text written for this lesson.
steps: Use tener for hair and eyes
Present a family and answer a question
discussion: Why "tiene el pelo castaño" but "es alta"?
Where do adjectives go in Spanish?
Which family member was easiest to describe?
What question did a classmate ask you?
study.product: Present a family of at least four members in Spanish, describing appearance, personality and age, and answer one question.

practice.q: Why use tener for hair but ser for personality?
practice.a: Spanish says you "have" hair and eyes but "are" a personality.
Adjectives agree in number with the noun.

practice.q: Translate: My brother is short and fun and has black eyes.
practice.a: Mi hermano es bajo y divertido y tiene los ojos negros.

exitTicket: Describe a family member's hair and eyes.

options: C) at the end of the sentence

items.answer: Es bajo, tiene el pelo negro y es divertido.

items.q: Explain tener vs ser in descriptions.
items.answer: Tener for hair and eyes; ser for personality and height.
